0.title: Course Introduction
0.content:
Vertical tasting is one of the most advanced disciplines in the wine world — tasting the same estate and the same plot over 5, 10 or 20 consecutive years, watching how wine transforms from a closed, youthful form into a complex, profound work of mature art. Loire Chenin Blanc is the world's most underrated white variety for ageing potential; a bottle of Vouvray Moelleux or Savennières can sleep in the cellar for 30–50 years, slowly telling the terroir story of the Layon valley or the Anjou schist.

Learning Objectives

🔬 Understand the chemistry of wine ageing

The evolution from primary to secondary to tertiary aromas, and the chemical mechanisms of tannin polymerisation and softening

📈 Grasp the three great Loire ageing curves

The specific "drinking windows" of Vouvray Moelleux, Savennières and Chinon Coteau

👃 Learn to identify mature aromas (Tertiary Aromas)

Judge a wine's depth of ageing from tertiary aromas such as beeswax, hazelnut and tobacco, and recognise the signs of decline of a wine "past peak"
1.title: The Chemistry of Wine Ageing: Three Evolutions of Aroma
1.highlights.0.title: Primary aromas
1.highlights.0.content: Aromas from the grape fruit itself: fresh fruit (strawberry, white peach, lime), floral notes (white flowers, violet), herbal notes (green pepper, mint). Young wines are dominated by primary aromas, noticeable immediately on opening.
1.highlights.1.title: Secondary aromas
1.highlights.1.content: Aromas from the winemaking process (fermentation, oak ageing): yeast (bread crumb, biscuit), cream (malolactic fermentation), vanilla (oak barrels). They become obvious in wines aged 1–5 years.
1.highlights.2.title: Tertiary aromas
1.highlights.2.content: Complex aromas formed during ageing: beeswax, honey (aged Chenin Blanc), leather, tobacco, mushroom (aged reds), toffee, almond, roasted hazelnut. They take 5–30 years to develop fully, and are the most precious discovery of a vertical tasting.
1.content:
The core of wine ageing is the chemistry of "slow oxidation." Trace oxygen in the bottle (through the cork) continually interacts with the phenolics, acids and esters in the wine, triggering a series of transformations of aroma and flavour:

🔬 Main chemical reactions during ageing

  • Esterification: acids (tartaric, malic acid) slowly combine with alcohol to form new ester compounds, the reason fruit aromas shift from "fresh fruit" to "dried fruit and preserved fruit"
  • Oxidation: polyphenols (anthocyanins, tannins) are slowly oxidised, so red wine colour shifts from bright purple-red → brick red → orange-brown, bringing tertiary aromas of leather, tobacco and earth
  • Maillard-like reactions: sugars and amino acids react over long ageing, forming complex aromas of toffee, roasted hazelnut and coffee
  • The role of acidity: high acidity (as in Chenin Blanc and Riesling) is a prerequisite for very long ageing — acidity slows the rate of oxidation, preventing the wine from "ageing too fast" and making 30–50 years of ageing possible
2.title: Vouvray Moelleux Vertical Tasting: A 30-Year Journey
2.content:
Taking a bottle of top Vouvray Moelleux (such as Domaine Huet "Le Haut-Lieu") as an example, we follow its evolution over 30 years:

🍑 1–3 years (infancy)

Appearance: pale golden yellow with a green sheen

Aromas: fresh apricot, white peach, apple blossom, acacia honey; primary aromas dominate, fresh and pure

Palate: clear sweetness, high acidity, youthful tension, with a mineral-salt note on the finish

Advice: drinkable, but possibly too simple; best to wait another 5 years

🍊 5–10 years (youth)

Appearance: golden yellow with an amber sheen

Aromas: dried apricot, baked pear, manuka honey, buttered toast; secondary aromas begin to integrate

Palate: sweet–acid balance more harmonious, texture beginning to turn silky, minerality more integrated

Advice: the first drinking window, suited to pairing with foie gras or blue cheese

🥇 15–25 years (golden age)

Appearance: deep golden yellow, amber rim

Aromas: beeswax, ginger, candied orange peel, toffee, hazelnut, smoky minerality — tertiary aromas fully developed

Palate: sweetness and acidity reach perfect balance, with a texture like liquid silk and a finish of 60 seconds or more

Advice: the optimal drinking window, paired with Époisses cheese or foie gras terrine

🍂 30 years+ (wisdom)

Appearance: amber-brown, with an orange-brown rim

Aromas: walnut, roasted almond, caramel, tea leaf, smoked wood — an oxidative complexity like Vin Jaune or Sherry

Palate: acidity still present but softer, sweetness almost imperceptible (masked by complexity), with a very long but quietening finish

Advice: taste on its own or with walnuts and aged cheese
3.title: Chinon & Savennières Vertical Ageing Compared
3.content:
🍷 Chinon Coteau (tuffeau slope) vertical ageing

Taking Charles Joguet "Clos de la Dioterie" as an example:

AgeColourAromasPalate state
1–3 yearsDeep rubyFresh violet, raspberry, green pepperTight, astringent tannins, not recommended for drinking
5–8 yearsRuby, with a brick-red rim beginning to appearDried flowers, strawberry jam, graphiteBeginning to integrate, worth trying
10–15 yearsBrick red + garnetLeather, dried rose, tobacco, pencil shavingsAt its best, with supple tannins
20 years+Orange-brownCinnamon, dried mushroom, tarStill powerful, but beginning to simplify

🏔️ Savennières dry white (Coulée de Serrant)

Taking Nicolas Joly "Coulée de Serrant" as an example:

AgeAromasPalate state
1–5 yearsMinerals, white flowers, lime peel — almost closedExtremely closed, not recommended to open
8–15 yearsBeeswax, acacia, smoky mineralityBeginning to open, astonishing minerality
20–30 yearsHazelnut, mushroom, iodine minerality, white truffleAt its best, unforgettable

The consensus of many tasters is that top Coulée de Serrant takes more than ten years to begin to open up.
4.title: Quick Quiz
4.questions.0.question: Which group is the most typical representative of "tertiary aromas" in wine ageing?
4.questions.0.explanation: Tertiary aromas form slowly during long bottle ageing, and include complex aromas such as beeswax, leather, tobacco, mushroom, toffee, dried fruit and earth. The first group is primary aromas (from the variety itself), the second is secondary aromas (from winemaking), and the fourth is also primary aromas.
4.questions.1.question: What is the most fundamental reason Vouvray Moelleux can age for so long?
4.questions.1.options.0: Because it has plenty of preservatives added
4.questions.1.options.1: Chenin Blanc's naturally very high acidity (pH 3.0–3.4) slows oxidation, preventing premature ageing and making 20–50 years of ageing possible
4.questions.1.options.2: Because it is aged in brand-new oak barrels, whose antioxidants protect the wine
4.questions.1.options.3: Because Vouvray's regulations set a minimum ageing period
4.questions.1.explanation: The fundamental reason for the very long ageing potential of Chenin Blanc (and Riesling) is its very high natural acidity (pH 3.0–3.4 or even lower). A high-acid environment suppresses oxidase activity and slows the rate of oxidation, keeping the wine fresh and lively in the bottle for decades. Residual sugar (in sweet wines) also gives extra protection.
